title: What €50,000 Buys in 2026: 140 Checked Homes, Country by Country
desc: We sorted every home on RealHunt by price. 46 of 140 cost €50,000 or less, and almost all of them are in three countries.
author: RealHunt Research
html:
€50,000 is roughly what a new mid-size car costs, or a deposit on a flat in most European cities. We wanted to know what it buys if you spend it on a whole house instead, so we sorted every home currently published on RealHunt by price.

The short answer: 46 of the 140 homes on the site cost €50,000 or less. They are not spread evenly. 29 are in Italy, 9 in Japan and 6 in Sweden. France and Denmark have one each. Spain, the United States, Canada and Mexico have none under that line.

Every home here passed the same check: a person looked at the photos and the listing, and anything that needs a new roof, is a ruin, is only land or has a single photo was left out. So these are cheap homes you could sleep in, not projects.

Italy: the most homes for the money

Italy has the cheapest home on the site, a stone house in a Lazio hill town for €12,000, about 55 minutes from Rome's Ciampino airport. Half of the 39 Italian homes cost €41,000 or less. At this price you are mostly buying in small inland villages: Tuscany, Lazio, Umbria and Abruzzo come up again and again. Expect thick stone walls, a small kitchen, and a piazza five minutes away on foot.

What the price hides: Italy's buying costs are the highest on our list. For a second home, registration tax is 9% of the cadastral value (a tax value that is usually well below the price), and the notary and registry add about €2,500. Our cost estimate adds roughly 10% plus €2,500 to be safe, so a €30,000 house is closer to €35,500 all in.

Japan: bigger houses, lower running costs

Japan's cheapest homes on RealHunt start at €18,400 and the middle of the list is €51,980. 9 of 18 are under €50,000. For that money the houses tend to be larger than in Italy, often with a garden, and many are near the coast in Wakayama, Kyoto prefecture and Okayama. Foreigners can own land and houses outright in Japan, with no residency needed to buy.

Sweden: where €50,000 is the entry ticket

Sweden's median on our list is €72,000, higher than Italy or Japan, and only 6 of 41 Swedish homes are under €50,000. But what you get is often a detached wooden house with a big plot, near a lake, with a wood stove. Anyone can buy in Sweden, and the only real buying cost is a 1.5% stamp duty. There is no notary.

North America starts higher

In the United States the cheapest move-in-ready home we have published is €65,428 (a brick row house in McKees Rocks, Pennsylvania, asking $75,000). Canada starts at €55,842 and Mexico at €50,575. Those markets have plenty of cheaper listings, but at the very bottom many are sold as investor projects: boarded windows, fire damage, or a plot with a trailer on it. They do not pass our quality rule.

What we take from this

If €50,000 is your hard ceiling, Italy is where you will have the most choice by far, Japan is where you get the most house, and Sweden is where you get the most land. Add 2% (Sweden) to 10% (Italy) on top for taxes and fees, and always pay for a survey before you sign.

You can see every home under €50,000 on one page: houses for sale under €50,000, or just the ones under €30,000.

title: How Many Months of Rent Would Buy You a Whole House?
desc: We divided the median price of homes on RealHunt by three monthly rents. At €1,200 a month, a typical Italian village house costs less than three years of rent.
author: RealHunt Research
html:
This is the comparison that surprises people most. If you pay €1,200 a month in rent, you hand over €14,400 a year. In three years that is €43,200, which is more than the median price of an Italian home on our site (€41,000).

That does not mean you should quit your lease tomorrow. A house in a village two hours from the nearest city is not the same thing as a flat near your job. But the comparison is useful because it puts a price you cannot picture (a house in another country) next to one you pay every month.

The table

We took the median price of the homes published on RealHunt in each country and divided it by three monthly rents: €800, €1,200 and €2,000. We did not use official rent figures for any city. Pick the column closest to what you pay.

CountryMedian home on RealHuntMonths at €800Months at €1,200Months at €2,000
Italy€41,000513420
Japan€51,980654326
Sweden€72,000906036
Mexico€80,9201016740
United States€85,9291077243
Canada€92,5521167746

Across all 140 homes the median is €61,280. At €1,200 a month that is 51 months of rent, a little over four years.

What the table leaves out

Buying costs come first. They range from about 2% of the price in Sweden to about 10% in Italy, plus fixed fees. On each home page we show the estimate for that exact price.

Then there is the cost of keeping a house. Council tax on a small Italian village home is often a few hundred euros a year. In Sweden and Canada, heating in winter is the big one. In the US, property tax is set by the county and is usually shown in the listing. None of this is close to rent, but it is not zero.

And there is the part no spreadsheet captures: whether you actually want to live there. The cheapest homes are cheap because people left those places. Some are coming back to life with remote workers and retirees; others are quiet for a reason. Visit before you buy. Stay a week, in winter if you can.

Try it with your own rent

On every home page on RealHunt there is a line that says how many months of rent the house is worth. It uses a rough average rent for the city your browser is in. It is a nudge, not financial advice, but it is a fair way to see these prices.

Start with the cheapest: homes under €30,000.

title: Cheap Houses in Sweden: What €22,000 to €99,000 Gets You
desc: 41 Swedish homes under €100,000, most of them red wooden houses on big plots near a lake. Where they are, what they cost to buy, and what to check.
author: RealHunt Research
html:
Sweden is the country people are most surprised by when they browse RealHunt. It has a reputation for being expensive, and in Stockholm it is. But 41 of the homes on our site are Swedish, all under €100,000, and most of them look like the picture you have in your head: a red wooden house with white corners, a garden, and a lake somewhere behind the trees.

Where the cheap ones are

Värmland, in the west near the Norwegian border, has the most homes on our list. After that come Småland, Dalarna, Skåne and Jönköping. These are forest and lake regions with small towns, not suburbs. Many houses are an hour or so from an airport: Karlstad, Växjö, Jönköping or Göteborg depending on where you are.

The cheapest Swedish home on the site is €22,000, a wooden house in the forest 550 metres from a lake. The median is €72,000. For that you usually get a detached house with a plot measured in thousands of square metres, not hundreds. Several come with a sauna, a guest cabin or a barn.

How buying works

This is where Sweden is easy. Anyone can buy a house, whether or not you live in the EU. There is no notary. The buyer pays a stamp duty (lagfart) of 1.5% of the price plus a small fixed fee to register the title, and a mortgage registration fee if you borrow. The seller pays the estate agent. On a €60,000 house your buying costs are roughly €1,000 to €2,000.

Sales usually run as open bidding through the agent. The asking price is a starting point, and popular houses can go above it. You sign a contract, pay a deposit of around 10%, and the rest on the day you get the keys.

What to check before you bid

Winter. Ask what heating the house has (wood, electric, a heat pump or geothermal) and what it cost to heat last winter. Several homes on our list mention geothermal or heat pumps, which bring the bills down a lot.

Water and drains. Country houses often have their own well and septic system. Ask when the septic tank was last emptied and whether the well water has been tested.

Access. A gravel road that is lovely in June can be hard work in January. Ask who clears the snow.

In Sweden the buyer is expected to inspect the house properly before buying, and hidden faults you could have found are usually your problem afterwards. Many sellers order an inspection report; read it, even with a translator, and consider your own.

title: Not Every Cheap House in Japan Is an Abandoned Akiya
desc: Stories about free houses in Japan usually show wrecks. These 18 homes start at €18,400 and you could move into them.
author: RealHunt Research
html:
You have probably seen the headlines: Japan has millions of empty houses, and some towns give them away. It is true. It is also why so many people are disappointed when they look closer. Most of the free and near-free houses need a new roof, new plumbing and months of work, and some are not worth saving.

So we set a different bar. The 18 Japanese homes on RealHunt all look like somewhere you could live now. Prices start at €18,400 and the middle of the list is €51,980.

What the money buys

At the bottom of the range you get older wooden houses in the countryside: a 100-year-old farmhouse with its own farmland, or a 1977 single-storey house with a sakura garden in Usuki, Oita, about 500 metres from the sea. Around €40,000 to €60,000 the houses are often renovated, with new kitchens and bathrooms, and several have sea views on the Seto Inland Sea or the Sea of Japan coast.

At the top, around €91,000, there is a Japanese-style single-storey house with an engawa (the wooden veranda) and a garden in Yugawara, a coastal hot spring town about 90 minutes from Tokyo.

Can a foreigner buy?

Yes. Japan lets foreigners own houses and land outright, with no visa or residency needed to buy. Buying costs add up to roughly 8% on top of the price: acquisition tax, registration, stamp duty and the agent's commission, which is capped by law. Owning a house does not give you a visa, so if you want to live there full time that is a separate question.

What to check

Age matters in Japan in a way it does not in Europe. Houses built before June 1981 were built to older earthquake rules. Many are fine and some have been reinforced, but ask. Ask too about the septic system, whether the land is freehold or leased, and what the fixed asset tax is each year (usually low for older rural houses).

Distance is the other thing. A house in a quiet coastal town can be two or three hours from a big city by train. That is the point for some buyers and a problem for others.

title: Italian Homes Near the Sea for Under €50,000: Where They Actually Are
desc: Cheap Italian houses are usually in inland hill towns. A few are close to the water. Here is where they are and what the catch is.
author: RealHunt Research
html:
Most of the cheap Italian homes you see online are in inland villages, and there is a reason: the coast is where Italians go on holiday, so that is where prices are high. But not everywhere. On RealHunt right now there are a handful of homes under €50,000 that are on the coast or a few minutes' drive from a beach, and they cluster in three places: Calabria, Sicily and Puglia.

Calabria

The toe of Italy has the longest coastline of any mainland region and some of the lowest prices. In Acquappesa, on the Tyrrhenian side, there is a one-bedroom place with a sea-view terrace for €39,000, about 2 km from the water. Further south in Falconara Albanese there is a three-room flat with a sea view for €41,000. Two more homes in Calabria, at €30,000 and €35,000, are listed as five minutes from the beach.

Sicily

In Marsala, on the west coast, a 135 m² apartment is €34,000, about 600 metres from the sea. That is €252 per square metre, the lowest on the site for an Italian home with a size in the listing. In Acquedolci, on the north coast near Messina, a two-level flat that was largely renovated is €49,000. There is also a sea-view home with an 87 m² panoramic terrace 20 minutes from Messina for the same price.

Puglia and Sardinia

Puglia has two whitewashed and vaulted houses around 20 to 25 minutes from the beach at €28,000 and €49,000. In Sardinia, a furnished tower house on four floors in a historic district is €35,000, about 3 km from the beaches.

The catch

These are mostly apartments or small village houses, not villas. Sea views at this price usually come with stairs, a small kitchen and a building that has seen a few decades. Summer is busy and some coastal towns are very quiet from November to March. And the costs of buying in Italy are high: plan for 10% on top, plus about €2,500 in fees.

Always ask for the APE (the energy certificate) and whether the property is "conforme": that what is built matches what is registered at the land registry. A good local geometra can check this for a few hundred euros, and it is worth every one.

All of them in one place: cheap houses by the sea in Italy. For the hill towns, see stone houses in Italy.

title: Move-In-Ready Houses in the US for Around $100,000
desc: We published 13 US homes that cost under €100,000 and do not need gutting. They start at $75,000. Here is where they are.
author: RealHunt Research
html:
Search for cheap houses in the US and you find thousands under $100,000. Open them and many are the same story: fire damage, boarded windows, "cash only, investor special". We went through them looking for the opposite, homes you could move into this month, and published 13 so far.

They are asking between $75,000 and $110,000. On RealHunt every price is in euros so homes in different countries can be compared; at the rate we used, that is €65,428 to €95,961.

Where they are

The Pittsburgh area comes up more than anywhere else. McKees Rocks, McKeesport and Clairton, old steel towns along the rivers, have brick houses from the early 1900s with updated kitchens for $75,000 to $98,500. West Virginia has two: a three-bedroom on a double lot in Huntington for $89,900, and a two-bedroom with a newer metal roof in Chapmanville for $95,000. Then Indiana, Ohio, Oklahoma, Arkansas, Texas, New York, and one condo near the beach in Little River, South Carolina.

What "move-in ready" means here

We only publish a US home if the photos show a kitchen and bathroom in working order, floors, walls and windows in good shape, and no sign of major damage. It is not an inspection. It is a first filter so you do not waste an afternoon on a house with a hole in the roof.

Buying as a foreigner

Anyone can buy a house in the US. You do not need residency or a visa. Buyer closing costs are usually 2% to 5% of the price: title insurance, escrow and recording fees. Property tax is charged every year by the county or town, often somewhere between 0.5% and 2% of the assessed value, and the listing usually shows it. Owning a home does not give you the right to live in the US; that is a separate visa question.

What to check

Get a home inspection. Ask about the age of the roof, the furnace and the water heater, which are the big bills in the first years. Check flood zone maps for houses near rivers. And look at the street on a map: in some of these towns, prices can change a lot from one block to the next.

See them all: homes in the United States.

title: Why We Say No to Most Cheap Houses
desc: A cheap house that needs €80,000 of work is not a cheap house. The rule we use to decide what goes on RealHunt, and why we turn most listings down.
author: RealHunt Research
html:
The internet is full of cheap houses. Most of them are cheap for a reason. The €1 houses in Italian villages come with an obligation to renovate, usually within three years, and the renovation costs far more than €1. The Japanese akiya you see in videos often need new roofs. And a lot of the American homes under $50,000 are listed for investors because they are not fit to live in.

RealHunt is for a different question: what can you buy for under €100,000 and live in, more or less as it is?

The rule

Every home is looked at by a person before it goes up. We say no to:

  • homes that clearly need major work: a new roof, rebuilt walls, no kitchen or bathroom
  • ruins and shells, however pretty the stone
  • land on its own, or land with a trailer or a shed
  • listings with one photo, or photos of the town instead of the house
  • anything over €100,000

Old is fine. Some of our favourite homes were built in the 1800s. What matters is that someone has looked after them.

In practice this means we turn down far more than we publish. Right now there are 140 homes on the site and 446 listings that were submitted or imported and turned down.

Where the homes come from

Some are found by our own research on public listing sites. Some come from people and accounts who post homes they have found, and every one goes through the same check. Signed-in members can open the original listing and contact the seller or agent directly. RealHunt is not an estate agent and does not sell the houses.

How the ranking works

The order on the front page comes from votes. Each week starts from zero, and the homes people vote for most rise to the top. There are no paid placements in the ranking. Where there is a sponsored card, it says so.

What we get wrong

Photos can flatter. Listings go out of date. A house that looks fine may have a problem only a survey will find. If you see a home that is sold or not what it seems, use the report button on its page and we will check it. And before you buy anything, anywhere, get an independent inspection and a local lawyer or notary.
